# How to study this reference

This book is a guide you return to, from a first definition through a checkable study. It is not a short textbook and it is not a tour of every algorithm. Each chapter is a reference entry: a card, the theory, a derivation, code, an experiment with a decision rule, and a project with a rubric. The same entry then splits into a beginner track, a university track, and a research track.

## Who it is for

A complete progression means different chapters make different demands.

| Track | What you do | What you skip |
|---|---|---|
| Beginner | The card, the code, and the smallest experiment. Learn the notation by using it. | Optional proofs and research extensions. |
| University | The derivation, the full experiment, and the project rubric. | Nothing in the main path of that chapter. |
| Research | The failure modes, a changed assumption, and a written limit on the claim. | The pretense that a benchmark name is a result. |

You can be a beginner in Volume 14 and at research depth in Volume 04. The track is about the chapter.

## How a session works

Ninety minutes is the default unit.

1. Read the reference card and restate the result in one sentence, including an assumption.
2. Read the theory and the derivation until you can point to the step that would fail if the assumption failed.
3. Run the code on the known case. If it fails, the experiment does not start.
4. Run the experiment and write the decision in `notes/`, with the metric and the command.
5. If the chapter's project is the day's work, leave a rerunnable folder, not only a plot.

A chapter is usable as a reference when you can look up the card and rerun the known case. It is university-complete when every layer is done. It is research-complete when you have written one way the assumption fails.

## What "comprehensive" means here

Every serious entry has four layers.

| Layer | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| Theory | What is true, under which assumptions, and what is not claimed? |
| Code | Can you implement the object and check a known case? |
| Experiment | What would change your mind, and did you measure it? |
| Project | Can someone else rerun the artifact and see the decision? |

A paragraph you highlighted and did not measure is not yet part of your reference. The book is long so that the path exists. Your notes become the reference when they are attached to the experiments.

## Suggested order

Read Volume 01 through Volume 07 in order the first time. Those volumes build notation, optimization, probability, inference, supervised baselines, and honest evaluation. After that, pick a path:

- **Representations.** Volumes 08, 09, 11, and 13.
- **Training and language.** Volumes 10, 12, and 17.
- **Decisions over time.** Volume 14, then Volume 17's agent chapter.
- **Operating a system.** Volume 15, then Volume 16.
- **Making a claim.** Volume 18, which you should open early as a way of taking notes and finish as a capstone.

Volume 18's upstream chapter says which external books to read beside this path. Those books stay in their own repositories.

## What this book will not do

It will not paste the Harvard CS249r textbook, Dive into Deep Learning, the Think series, or the Hugging Face course into these chapters. Those works have their own licenses, described on the upstream page. It will not call a free PDF an open license. It will not treat a leaderboard number as a definition of understanding.

When a chapter says to refuse a claim, that refusal is part of the result.
